name: Uma Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for doing this, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a company of about eighty people that makes plug-ins for small online shops: the checkout box, the stock counter, the little 'only 3 left' badge. I'm on the front-end team, which means I build the parts customers see, and most days I'm making the checkout page look right on every kind of phone. Yesterday I spent four hours on a button that went off the edge of the screen on one old phone model.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing our checkout on a real shop's website, like the candle shop my sister buys from. What wears me out is code reviews, where a senior goes through my work line by line, because I usually get eight or nine comments and the others get two. I'm still learning, and my pay shows it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Tomas, who runs a shift at the supermarket's big warehouse outside town. Between us we cover rent and his car loan, and that's about it; we've got maybe two or three weeks of money saved. There aren't many software jobs around here, so I'm careful not to upset anyone at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected, honestly. The AI chat tool I use now and then is handy for small things, like explaining an error, but it never fixed the hard stuff. I wouldn't make a big deal of it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means things carry on, which is fine but not comfortable. I'm still the junior with the most comments in code review, on low pay, in a town with three tech employers. My worry was never really AI, it's that I'm not improving fast enough to get a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and ask my lead, Priya, for one clear goal to work toward a pay rise by next year. I'd use the AI tool a bit more for checking my own code before review, so I get fewer comments. Tomas and I would try to pay off his car loan early, because that's the bill that hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. Nothing's on fire, but we live close to the edge and that doesn't change with a plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'close to the edge' look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the boiler broke and the landlord took three weeks to fix it, and we bought two heaters on a credit card. We still haven't cleared that card. That's the edge: one thing breaks and it takes six months to recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about AI Plateau that would actually help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If the AI tool catches my silly mistakes before a senior sees them, I look better in reviews. That's the boring kind of help, but boring help is what I need.

say: AI turned out about as I **expected**: handy for **small things**, never the hard stuff.
I wouldn't make a **big deal** of the plateau online.
think: My worry was never AI; it's **not improving fast** enough for a raise.
I'm still the junior with the **most review comments**, in a town with three tech employers.
do: Ask Priya for **one clear goal** toward a pay rise next year.
Use the AI tool to **check my code** before review.
feel: **Quietly uneasy**: nothing's on fire, but they live close to the **edge**.
S0.quote: One thing breaks and it takes six months to recover.
fieldNote: Uma's pressure is **thin money** and slow progress, which a plateau doesn't touch.
She wants **boring help** from AI, like catching mistakes before review.
The **credit card** from last winter's heaters still isn't cleared.

steps.text: Ask Priya for one clear goal toward a raise next year
Run the AI tool over her code before each review
Overpay Tomas's car loan each month to clear it early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to use it where it works and be careful where it doesn't. Front-end is a lot of repetitive layout work, so I'd expect it to change fast. I'd say that at work and keep it calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think juniors like me get squeezed first. If the tools can build a checkout layout, the company needs fewer people building them, and a senior with AI does what I do. There are three tech employers in town, and they'd all be doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I see the other front-end devs using the tools properly, which would be fast, I'd copy them and learn the same tools in the first few months. I'd try to move toward the part of the job the tools are worse at, talking to shop owners about what they need, and ask Priya if I can sit in on customer calls. And we'd stop eating out and put that into savings, maybe eighty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see what's coming, and I can see I'm at the back of the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Tomas's job feel safer in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For now, yes. The card said robots spread into hands-on work more slowly, and he's on the warehouse floor. It's odd, because my partner's warehouse job always felt like the one at risk, and now it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd copy the others. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not the strongest, and if I go first with a tool and it breaks a checkout, that's on me. If the seniors go first, I learn from their mistakes. It's not brave, but it's sensible.

say: Use AI **where it works** and be careful where it doesn't.
Front-end layout work is **repetitive**, so I'd expect it to change fast.
think: Juniors get **squeezed first** when a senior with AI can do my work.
All **three tech employers** in town would be cutting the same way.
do: Copy the seniors and learn their **AI tools** in the first few months.
Ask to sit in on **customer calls** with shop owners.
Stop eating out and save about **eighty a month**.
feel: **Anxious**, seeing what's coming and feeling at the back of the **queue**.
S1.quote: My partner's warehouse job always felt like the one at risk, and now it's mine.
fieldNote: Uma moves **second on purpose**, letting seniors make the first mistakes.
She aims for **customer-facing** work the tools do less well.
The household's risk **flips**: her desk job now looks weaker than Tomas's warehouse job.

steps.text: Learn the AI layout tools the senior front-end devs use
Ask Priya to join customer calls with shop owners
Stop eating out and save eighty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments to do something sensible quickly: support for people losing jobs, and rules on how fast firms can cut. Not banning it, that won't work. Just slowing the fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job goes in 2028, and Tomas's goes in 2031 when the robots arrive in warehouses. So we get three years where he earns and I don't, and then neither of us does. I've never had to think about both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job as long as I can and learn the tools well, since that buys months. I'd look hard at hands-on work for the three-year gap: Tomas says the warehouse always needs forklift drivers, so I'd get the licence this spring, which costs about three hundred. We'd cancel everything that isn't rent, food and the car loan, and talk to my parents about moving in if it comes to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie there working out which month the money runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A forklift licence after a software diploma. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, but practical. Three years of wages is three years, and Tomas could show me the ropes. I'd feel a bit embarrassed telling my old classmates, but they'd be in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister not to start the coding course she's been looking at. That would be hard, because I talked her into it. I'd tell her to find something where people need a person in the room.

say: Governments should give **job-loss support** and rules on how fast firms can cut.
**Banning AI** won't work; just slow the fall.
think: My job goes in **2028**, and Tomas's goes in 2031 when **warehouse robots** arrive.
For the first time I have to think about **both incomes** at once.
do: Learn the tools well to **keep my job** a few months longer.
Get a **forklift licence** this spring for about three hundred.
Cancel everything except rent, food and the car loan, and **ask my parents** about moving in.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake working out which month the **money runs out**.
S2.quote: I'd tell my sister not to start the coding course she's been looking at.
fieldNote: Uma uses the **3-year robot gap** directly: a forklift licence to work beside Tomas.
She sees the household losing **both incomes** in sequence.
Steering her **sister away** from coding hurts, because Uma encouraged it.

steps.text: Learn the AI coding tools to stay employed a few months longer
Get a forklift licence this spring for about three hundred
Cancel every bill except rent, food and the car loan
Ask her parents if she and Tomas could move in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if companies and governments start now. Train people, plan the cuts, don't drop it on people overnight. Middle-of-the-road stuff, but it's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I have a few years in software, then 2031 hits my job, and 2034 hits Tomas's. That's actually enough time for one of us to retrain into something solid. I think it should be me, because my job goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at work and get properly good with the AI tools by 2027, because there'd be a few years of work using them. I'd start an evening course in something hands-on and people-facing; I've been thinking about dental nursing, because my aunt does it and the clinic always needs people. We'd save harder and aim for three months of money by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan, and that helps. I sleep better with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dental nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's hands-on, you're with people, and my aunt says the dentist she works for can't find staff. Robots for dental nursing only come around 2034, and even then I think patients would want a person holding their hand. Also, the course is part-time over two years, which I can do around work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the plan if the company cuts juniors early, say in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go into dental nursing early, on a trainee wage, and we'd be very tight. That's why the three months of savings matters. Without it, an early cut would be a disaster.

say: Five years is **enough time** if companies and governments **start now**.
Train people and plan the cuts instead of dropping them on people overnight.
think: My job goes in **2031** and Tomas's in **2034**.
One of us has time to **retrain**, and it should be me, since my job goes first.
do: Get properly good with the **AI tools** by 2027.
Start an evening **dental nursing** course, part-time over two years.
feel: **Anxious**, but she sleeps better **with a plan**.
S3.quote: Robots for dental nursing only come around 2034, and even then I think patients would want a person holding their hand.
fieldNote: Uma plans the household **as a pair**: she retrains first because her job goes first.
Her aunt's job shows her a **hands-on, people** role that lasts.
She knows an **early cut** would wreck the plan without savings.

steps.text: Get confident with the AI tools by 2027
Start a part-time dental nursing course in the evenings
Build three months of savings by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this sensibly. Retraining, support, careful rules. I'd probably say it a bit more confidently than the other versions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be all right. I'd have years to get better at my job, maybe get to mid-level, save something, and then choose where to go before 2036. Tomas's warehouse job lasts until about 2039, so we'd have a long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For now, I'd carry on and learn the AI tools as they become normal at work, over the next year or two. I'd aim for a mid-level role by 2029 and pay off the car loan and the credit card. Around 2031 I'd look again at dental nursing or something similar, once I can see which jobs are really holding up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way. It's on my mind, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Tomas change any life plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. We'd talked about getting a bigger place and maybe a dog. With ten years, I think we'd still do that, just a bit later, once the debts are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in feeling you have plenty of time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. I'd want to write the plan down with dates, like I do with sprint tasks at work, the two-week chunks we plan our work in. Without a written plan, year eight comes and I'm still on the same checkout button.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time** to do this sensibly.
Retraining, support and **careful rules** would be what I'd push for.
think: I'd have years to reach **mid-level**, save something and choose before 2036.
Tomas's warehouse job lasts until **about 2039**, so we'd have a long run.
do: Learn the AI tools as they become **normal at work**.
Reach a **mid-level role** by 2029 and clear the car loan and card.
feel: **Uneasy** in a normal way: on her mind, but not keeping her up.
S4.quote: Without a written plan, year eight comes and I'm still on the same checkout button.
fieldNote: With ten years, Uma's household looks **secure enough**; plans for a bigger place survive.
She guards against **complacency** by planning in dated chunks, like work sprints.
Debt, not AI, is the **first thing** she'd tackle.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools as the front-end team adopts them
Clear the car loan and the heater credit card

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my job and then Tomas's, three years apart, before we've saved anything. What would help is short, paid courses for hands-on jobs, so I could earn while I train, and support that bridges the gap between jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like being a couple where the risk swaps around. For years everyone said warehouse jobs would go first. Now my software job looks like the fragile one, and I'm the one who went to college.

headlineQuote: For years everyone said warehouse jobs would go first. Now my software job looks like the fragile one, and I'm the one who went to college.
portrait: Uma, 27, builds **checkout screens** for a company making plug-ins for small online shops.
She lives with Tomas, a **warehouse shift lead**, with two or three weeks of savings and a car loan.
She adopts AI **after the seniors** do, learning from their mistakes rather than going first.
In the AGI pictures she plans around **two incomes**: hers ends first, Tomas's three years later.
Her fallbacks are a **forklift licence** in the fast version and dental nursing when there's more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which takes her job and then Tomas's before they've saved anything.
whatWouldHelp: Short, **paid courses** for hands-on jobs, plus support that bridges the **gap**.
